objetivo.en: Ask basic questions with qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto and cuál, written with their accent mark.

nota.en: Also written without an accent mark (que) when it doesn't ask a question.
Say DÓN-de, with the force on the first syllable.
It agrees with the noun: cuánto, cuánta, cuántos, cuántas.
Asks for one option among several.
A feminine word that takes el: el aula.

explicacion.en: Question words always carry an accent mark: dónde, qué, quién, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, cuál. Without it, the word is not a question word.
Cuánto changes to match the noun: cuántos estudiantes (masculine plural), cuántas profesoras (feminine plural).
Use qué es to ask for a definition (“What is this?”). Use cuál es to ask which one among several (“Which is your room?”).

titulo.en: Sound of the day: stress and the accent mark

texto.en: In Spanish, a written accent mark (called a tilde) shows which syllable you say with the most force. Every question word has one: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, cuál. Say them with energy on the marked vowel: DÓN-de, CUÁN-do, CÓ-mo, CUÁN-to. Qué, quién and cuál have only one syllable, so just say them firmly and clearly. The accent mark also separates a question word from its plain look-alike: que, donde and como, without an accent mark, are not asking a question. Keep every vowel short and pure, as you practiced in the first lesson.

Spanish has seven basic question words, and they always carry an accent mark: ¿qué? (what), ¿quién? (who), ¿dónde? (where), ¿cuándo? (when), ¿cómo? (how), ¿cuánto? (how much, how many) and ¿cuál? (which). The question opens with ¿ and closes with ?, and the verb comes next: there is no “do” as in English. With cuánto, the noun goes right after it: ¿Cuántos estudiantes hay? Use quién for people and qué for things. ¿Qué es esto? asks for a definition (“What is this?”), while ¿Cuál es el aula? asks which one among several (“Which one is the room?”). Cuánto agrees with the noun it goes with: ¿Cuántos estudiantes hay? (masculine plural), ¿Cuántas profesoras hay? (feminine plural). In ¿Dónde es la clase?, the class is an event, so Spanish uses es (ser) to ask where it takes place. Emma uses usted with her teacher: «Profesora, ¿dónde es la clase?»
Each one has an accent mark. Tap each phrase to hear it.

objetivo.en: Count from 21 to 100 and say other people's ages.

nota.en: One word from 21 to 29: veinti- + the unit.
The t is crisp, not “ch” as in tree; the r is a quick tap.
The ch sounds like the ch in chair.
It describes a noun: el aula es grande.

explicacion.en: From 31 on, put y between the tens and the unit: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, cincuenta y siete.
From 21 to 29, the number is written as one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veinticinco.
Spanish uses tener (to have) for age: Tengo veinticinco años, not soy.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: c, z and s sound like s

texto.en: In Latin American Spanish, the letter s, the letter z and the letters c before e or i all sound like an English s. So cincuenta sounds like “seen-KWEN-tah”, sesenta like “seh-SEN-tah” and cien like “syen”. The letter c before a, o or u is a hard k, as in cuarenta (“kwah-REN-tah”). Remember to keep every vowel short and pure: don't glide into a second sound. Say them slowly: cincuenta, sesenta, cien, veinticinco.

From 21 to 29, each number is one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veinticinco, veintinueve (veintidós, veintitrés and veintiséis carry an accent mark). The tens are treinta (30), cuarenta (40), cincuenta (50), sesenta (60), setenta (70), ochenta (80) and noventa (90). From 31 on, you say the tens, then y, then the unit, as three separate words: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, cincuenta y siete. One hundred is cien. Before a noun, uno becomes un: treinta y un años. To say someone's age, use tener: Tengo veinticinco años (I'm twenty-five), Rosa tiene cincuenta y siete años. To ask, use ¿Cuántos años tienes? (tú) or ¿Cuántos años tiene? (usted, or about a third person). Remember: Spanish says “I have twenty-five years”, not “I am twenty-five”.
Tap each number to hear it.

objetivo.en: Ask for and give a phone number, an email address and an address to open an account.

nota.en: The word used in Latin America.
The single r is a quick tap, like the tt in “butter”.
Say it aloud for @ in an email.
Say it aloud for . in an email.
For a young woman, with or without her name: señorita García.

explicacion.en: To ask for a piece of data (a number, an address), Spanish uses cuál es, not qué es: ¿Cuál es tu número?
Tu goes with tú (friends, people your age). Su goes with usted (older people, an operator): ¿Cuál es su número?

explicacion.en: In Spanish you say the symbols in Spanish: punto for the dot and arroba for @.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: r and rr

texto.en: The letter r is called “erre”. A single r between vowels is a quick tap of the tongue, like the tt in American “butter”: número, cero, dirección. A double rr is a trill, a strong vibration of the tongue: arroba, correo. A single r at the beginning of a word is also trilled, as in the name Rosa. Practice the difference slowly: número (tap) and correo, arroba (trill). Keep the vowels short and pure.

titulo.en: Giving your phone number and email

texto.en: To ask for contact information, use ¿Cuál es…? with tu (tú) or su (usted): ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono? with a friend, ¿Cuál es su número de celular? with an operator or an older person. Answer with Mi número es… A phone number is said digit by digit, usually in groups: 099 000 0042 is “cero nueve nueve, cero cero cero, cero cero cuatro dos”. In an email address, say arroba for @ and punto for the dot: emma.garcia@ejemplo.com is “emma punto garcia arroba ejemplo punto com”. To give your address, say Vivo en… and the neighborhood. In Latin America, el celular is a cell phone, and el correo (short for el correo electrónico) is email.
Phone numbers are said one digit at a time. Tap each word to hear it.

objetivo.en: Answer in the negative with no… nada, no… nadie and no… nunca.

nota.en: The d between vowels is soft: NAH-tha.
No estudio nada, solo hablo con Rosa.

explicacion.en: When nadie, nada or nunca come after the verb, the verb also needs no. Unlike English, the double negative is correct in Spanish.
In Spanish you speak with someone: hablar con. So “I don't talk to anyone” is No hablo con nadie.
When nunca or nadie comes before the verb, don't add no: Nunca hablo inglés, or No hablo inglés nunca.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the soft d

texto.en: Between vowels, the Spanish d is soft: the tongue barely touches the back of the teeth, and the sound is close to the th in English “this”, but lighter. Say it in nada (NAH-tha) and nadie (NAH-thyeh). At the beginning of a word, or after n or l, the d is firmer, closer to an English d, as in ¿dónde? Keep the vowels short and pure.

titulo.en: Answering in the negative: no… nada, no… nadie, no… nunca

texto.en: In English, a double negative is a mistake (“I don't study nothing”). In Spanish it is the rule. When the negative word nada (nothing), nadie (nobody) or nunca (never) comes after the verb, you also put no before the verb: No estudio nada (I don't study anything). No hablo con nadie (I don't talk to anyone). No hablo francés nunca (I never speak French). With people, Spanish uses con: con nadie. When nadie or nunca comes before the verb, you don't add no: Nunca hablo francés. Nadie habla francés en casa. Both orders mean the same: Nunca hablo francés and No hablo francés nunca.
You already know these verbs from earlier lessons. Here they are again, because you will use them with the negative words. Tap each one to hear it.

objetivo.en: Ask someone to repeat or to speak more slowly and say that you don't understand, with tú or usted.

nota.en: Learn it as a set phrase for now.
The polite way to ask someone to repeat.
One month = un mes. Por doce meses = for twelve months.

explicacion.en: With an older person or someone you don't know well, use usted: ¿Puede repetir? Use ¿Puedes repetir? only with friends and people your age.
Don't use the infinitive after “I”: the verb must change. Say No entiendo, not no entender.
After ¿Puede…? the second verb stays in the infinitive: ¿Puede repetir? ¿Puede hablar?

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the silent h

texto.en: The letter h is always silent in Spanish: it makes no sound at all. Hablar sounds like “ah-BLAR”, hola like “OH-lah” and ahora like “ah-OH-rah”. Don't breathe out as you do in English “hello”. Keep every vowel short and pure.

titulo.en: Asking someone to repeat or slow down

texto.en: When you don't understand, you can say No entiendo (I don't understand) and ask for help. With usted (an operator, an older person, someone you don't know), say ¿Puede repetir, por favor? (Can you repeat that, please?) or ¿Puede hablar más despacio? (Can you speak more slowly?). With tú (a friend, someone your age), say ¿Puedes repetir? and ¿Puedes hablar más despacio? You can also say just Más despacio, por favor, or Otra vez, por favor (one more time). To ask what someone said, use ¿Cómo dice? with usted and just ¿Cómo? with tú. For now, learn ¿Puede…? / ¿Puedes…? and no entiendo as ready-made phrases: you will study how these verbs work in later lessons. Remember that the infinitive repetir stays the same after puede.
